title: Glen Affric sees first wild-born beavers in 400 years
description: Image source, Trees for LifeImage caption, One of at least two beaver kits known to have been born at Glen AffricConservationists say Glen Affric in t
body: Image source, Trees for LifeImage caption, One of at least two beaver kits known to have been born at Glen AffricConservationists say Glen Affric in the Highlands has its first wild-born beavers since the animals died out in Scotland more than 400 years ago.Findhorn-based charity Trees for Life said there were at least two babies, called kits, known to have been born at Loch Beinn a Mheadhoin following the release of seven beavers in October and a family of four in February.Beavers were first reintroduced to Scotland in 2009, but there have been a number of illegal releases of the animals.Trees for Life has been working on a rewilding project with Forestry and Land Scotland (FLS), which manages the 43,500-acre reserve in the glen.Previously, wild-born beavers were spotted in the Cairngorms following licensed releases of adult animals.Glen Affric, near Cannich, is a large area of woodland, lochs, hills and mountains.Trees for Life said the Glen Affric kits were likely to have been born in May or June, before first emerging from their lodge over the past few weeks.The charity's beaver management officer, Tobias Leask, said: "These beaver kits symbolise a wildlife success story four centuries in the making, and how nature can recover when we give it a chance."Seeing them for the first time is something I'll never forget. It was one of those rare moments when you realise you're witnessing history."Image source, Chris AldridgeImage caption, Families of beavers were released in Glen Affric in October and FebruaryThe 11 released beavers had been relocated under licence by NatureScot from farmland in Tayside.Dr Roisin Campbell-Palmer, head of restoration at the Beaver Trust, said the arrival of the kits suggested the animals had settled well into their new surroundings.She added: "Every reintroduction requires careful planning and close monitoring after release, so it is hugely rewarding to see the animals adapting so successfully."This achievement reflects the commitment and collaboration of everyone involved and provides further evidence that well-managed translocations can support the responsible restoration of beavers across Scotland in line with the Scottish government's National Beaver Strategy."

schema.headline: Glen Affric sees first wild-born beavers in 400 years

title: Swansea chaplain dubbed Prime Minister Andy Burnham lookalike
description: A woman dubbed a lookalike of the new prime minister is "leaning into" the comparisons and has changed her name to "Mandy Burnham" on social media. Em
body: A woman dubbed a lookalike of the new prime minister is "leaning into" the comparisons and has changed her name to "Mandy Burnham" on social media. Emma Roberts from Swansea said she thinks "it's the eyebrows and the glasses" that make the resemblance to Andy Burnham, so much so that even her own mother agrees with the TikTok commentators who have pointed that out.She said it was "a bit of fun", but didn't expect to go viral.Roberts said the prime minister was "clearly a good communicator but it had only been one week" - although she said his tea-making skills were an "abomination".The Quaker chaplain usually posts about religion on social media, but said people would comment on her posts describing her as the Labour leader's doppelgänger."This just went on and on, and two more TikToks went viral and ended up with a quarter of a million views, and then someone said change your name to Mandy Burnham, so I thought why not?"The 54-year-old added that Burnham sounded like a "decent bloke" and she was keen to speak with him about his Catholic upbringing."I don't know him, but he sounds decent," she said adding that she "loved his pub snacks video"."On the whole his communication strategy has been very good but one of the abominations that he talks about is putting milk in with the teabag first. I mean he needs a talking to."That is just awful."

schema.headline: Swansea chaplain dubbed Prime Minister Andy Burnham lookalike

title: Nine killed in strikes on Kyiv, as Ukraine sinks Russian ship
description: At least nine people have been killed and dozens injured in Russian ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said
body: At least nine people have been killed and dozens injured in Russian ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said. Moscow has escalated deadly ballistic missile attacks on Kyiv recently, prompting Zelensky to say that missile interceptors are urgently needed.The strikes come two days after a suspected Russian cruise missile landed in Poland during a widespread attack on Ukraine that killed at least eight people, including six members of one family.Separately, Ukrainian drones sank a Russian-owned container ship in the Black Sea on Saturday. Moscow said all 17 crew were rescued. Kyiv's Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the capital had come under a ballistic missile attack on Saturday, with AFP reporting more than 10 explosions. Fires broke out across the city and power cuts were reported in some areas.Klitschko said a residential building in Shevchenkivskyi was partially destroyed, trapping people inside. The emergency services said at least seven people were killed in a strike in the Darnytskyi district. Another 14 were injured, including two children, it reported.In Solomyanskyi district, two people died and eight were injured, including two children, as a five-storey residential building was partially destroyed, officials said.A missile landed near the Lithuanian embassy, breaking windows and scattering debris in the compound, Lithuania's foreign ministry said.Zelensky said in a post on X that the sanctioned 100,000-tonne capacity container ship Yanina had been "sent to the bottom". Moscow confirmed the attack in a statement from state-owned nuclear operator Rosatom, which owns the ship. Rosatom said it had been transporting civilian goods including frozen food and construction materials, adding that the attack took place 130 miles (209km) from Novorossiysk."Such an attack cannot be interpreted as anything other than piracy and robbery," Rosatom's CEO Alexey Likhachev said, adding that all 17 crew members were in a "satisfactory" condition.Ukraine has targeted Russian-flagged ships in the Black Sea since Russia's full-scale invasion of the country in 2022. The attack on Kyiv comes after Zelensky met President Donald Trump in Washington DC earlier this week to urge the US to grant Ukraine a licence to produce Patriot interceptor missiles.Asked about the missiles during a cabinet meeting at the Camp David retreat on Friday, Trump said the US had not agreed to Ukraine building Patriot missiles but that talks were ongoing.He said the US had to be "very careful about letting somebody build them".Emphasising concerns about sharing advanced US weaponry, Trump called it "a big step".Trump's latest comments regarding Patriot missiles come weeks after he offered to give Ukraine the right to produce them.As Russia has stepped up its air attacks, Ukraine has run low on supplies of Patriots, which remain the only weapon in its arsenal capable of downing ballistic missiles.

schema.headline: Nine killed in strikes on Kyiv, as Ukraine sinks Russian ship

title: 'Our hearts are in ruins,' Savannah Guthrie says after kidnapped mother's ransom notes released
description: Police in Arizona have released two ransom notes in the hope the public can help identify whoever abducted the mother of US news presenter Savannah Gu
body: Police in Arizona have released two ransom notes in the hope the public can help identify whoever abducted the mother of US news presenter Savannah Guthrie.The first note, which is treated as apparently credible, demanded millions of dollars in Bitcoin. The other claimed Nancy Guthrie died shortly after she was abducted from her home near Tucson six months ago.The Pima County Sheriff's Office say they cannot verify her death, and the investigation remains active. "Our hearts are in ruins," Guthrie said on Saturday.Officials released the two notes on Friday, asking the public for help identifying the writer, whose "distinct linguistic characteristics may be recognisable".Investigators believe that Nancy Guthrie, who was aged 84 when she was last seen on 31 January, was taken against her will from her home, but they have not shared a possible motive or arrested a suspect.On Saturday morning Savannah Guthrie wrote on Instagram: "We have lived every moment, every breath, and every heartbeat in agony and despair.""Every day, we wake up and try to be strong and go on - because that's what our joyful and resilient Mom taught us to do. But make no mistake - our hearts are in ruins."The ransom notes were addressed to Savannah Guthrie and the Guthrie family, and sent to a local TV station in Tucson, Arizona, in the days after Nancy Guthrie disappeared, according to the sheriff. "A friend, family member, coworker, classmate, or acquaintance may recognise these patterns of expression and possess information that could help identify the individual responsible," the sheriff's office said in a statement.The first note, which was received on 2 February, began: "Hello Savannah, we have your mother Nancy. She is safe but scared. She will be held for ransom and once payment is received she will be released unharmed. We will be holding her for a maximum of 7 days. You will need to send bitcoin in the amount of $4 million USD before 5PM on Thursday the 5th."If payment is not received, the ransom will be increased to 6 million USD which will need to be paid by 5PM on Monday the 9th. Once payment is received to the bitcoin address below she will be released within 12 hours of deposit to a safe drop off location back in Tucson. If payment is not recieved [sic] by the last deadline on Monday the 9th at 5PM, she will be killed."Your mother is aware of this and her life is in your hands. It is in the best interest of everyone to have this completed as soon as possible. "You will not be able to contact me from here on out, there will be no negotiation. Do not play games, law enforcement will not be able to help you," the note continued.After what appears to be a redacted sentence, it ends: "She had a white smart watch on the floor of the foot of her bed and the white flood light in backyard was destroyed."Nancy Guthrie, who was taking daily medication, vanished after relatives dropped her off at her home on the evening of Saturday 31 January.Police were contacted when she failed to show up the following morning at a friend's house to watch a virtual Sunday church service.Four days after the first note, the second arrived: "Guthrie Family, we did not fully grasp the seriousness of her physical condition. We never intended to hurt her, that was not our intention."She perished shortly after she was taken. We believe it was heart related. She is buried in nature now."Nothing you could have done could have changed the outcome. We want your family to know this and hope you all can find peace. We are truly sorry."After the second note, Savannah Guthrie - one of the most famous TV presenters in the US - took to Instagram on 7 February to respond."We received your message and we understand," Guthrie said at the time. "We beg you now to return our mother to us... This is very valuable to us, and we will pay."Earlier this week, Guthrie again released a video calling for the kidnappers to "do the right thing" and reveal the location of her mother.In her social media post on Saturday, Savannah Guthrie said she and her family were "desperate" and "begging for help". Alongside a photo of her smiling mother, Guthrie wrote they were determined to "find out what happened to her, so that we can give her the dignity of a proper goodbye — a celebration of her remarkable life that she so deserves".She urged anyone who knows or suspects something to come forward, saying tips can be made anonymously and a reward for information leading to her recovery remains available.

schema.headline: 'Our hearts are in ruins,' Savannah Guthrie says after kidnapped mother's ransom notes released

title: He bought a fitness supplement online to bulk up, but ended up losing his mind
description: Daniel Murphy thought he was taking a safe and tested dietary supplement that would help him put on muscle in the gym.But over the following two years
body: Daniel Murphy thought he was taking a safe and tested dietary supplement that would help him put on muscle in the gym.But over the following two years, his mental health spiralled to such a degree he ended up in a state of psychosis in which he believed his wife was trying to steal his business and his mother-in-law was going to kill him.Unknown to Daniel, the daily pills he had been taking had been mixed with testosterone.The 32-year-old is one of 54,000 consumers listed in a case against a multimillion-pound peptide company based in the US, which sold its products around the world.The owner of Paradigm Peptides, Matthew Kawa, was jailed for five years and 10 months on Thursday after he admitted deliberately selling unapproved medicines, trying to deceive people about what they were and illegally bringing the products into the country. His sister, Jennifer Stechkober, who also pleaded guilty to selling unapproved medicines, was sent to prison for a year and four months.Both admitted they had lied about where the pills were sourced, their purity and their company's testing procedures. Despite claiming the supplements were manufactured in the US, they were actually imported from China, India and several other countries. The pair also faked certificates of analysis, the documents that prove the safety and quality of a product.Paradigm Peptides' website had stated it "stringently" tested all their products to ensure "efficacy, purity and potency", but the pair admitted not testing or analysing any of the products they sold, so they had not been aware they had been mixed with testosterone.Testosterone is a steroid hormone, which the body naturally produces. It drives physical development, builds muscle, and controls sex drive, primarily in males, but it also supports health in females. There is a synthetic version which doctors can prescribe, but which can cause liver damage, serious psychiatric effects and heart and respiratory problems if taken without medical oversight. It can also cause infertility in men and increase the risk of testicular cancer.The Paradigm Peptides case is the biggest to rock the industry, an unregulated market which has exploded into the mainstream over the past 18 months.Peptides are short chains of amino acids that our bodies produce and have long been used to treat medical conditions, including diabetes. More recently, they are being used in weight-loss drugs - GLP-1s. Another type of drug sold by Paradigm Peptides was SARMs - Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators - which target specific tissues to increase muscle and bone mass.Both these types of unregulated injectable drugs have become increasingly popular in the online wellness community - including among many young influencers.Social media is inundated with people extolling the virtues of various substances - such as BPC-157, GHK-CU and TB 500 - all of which purport to help build muscle mass, help with tissue recovery, or improve skin health. They are not licensed, can only be sold for testing purposes and are not suitable for human consumption.Three years ago, Murphy says he was in a good place. He was married to Laura, and they had built a "very stable, consistent, beautiful life" in the Smoky mountains in Knoxville, Tennessee.Murphy had lost 130 pounds (59kg) and had "completed a major health transformation" through diet and exercise."I wasn't into gym culture - I wasn't a big gym bro or anything," he explains. "But after I had lost all that weight, I wanted to start building muscle and these supplements seemed like a safe way of doing that."Murphy thought he was taking a daily dose of SARMs. Like peptides, they are not approved for human use and are seen as experimental drugs with a risk of serious liver damage, thrombosis and heart problems.Murphy says he felt safe taking them because they were clearly labelled a "dietary supplement" and Paradigm claimed it had a contract with the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on various blogs, but this was not true."Like other victims, I trusted that the products were safe," he says. "They presented everything as research backed with claims of 99% purity - it was all a lie."Murphy started taking Paradigm's SARMs in January 2023. During the first few months, he says they seemed to be having a positive effect: he was able to do longer workouts and had more energy. Encouraged by fake research articles he had read on Paradigm Peptides's website, he then started taking other products too.Insomnia and mania began to set in - and that triggered him, he says, to "burn down" everything he had built - his marriage, his friendships, and his business.During the court proceedings, consultant psychiatrist and pharmacologist, Dr Erik Messamore, gave evidence to confirm that he believed Murphy had been suffering from a steroid-induced psychosis.As Murphy's life spun out of control, unknown to him, the FDA was already investigating Paradigm Peptides. It had been sending warning letters to the company since 2020 telling it to stop selling unapproved drugs. By September 2023, the FDA had seized SARMs products from Paradigm to carry out tests on them. It turned out, all the supplements had been mixed with testosterone.But it would take another six months before the FDA closed the business down.In the UK, Adam Taylor, professor of anatomy at Lancaster University, has been watching cases like this closely, as the scientific community continues to raise the alarm on this market which operates in a legal and regulatory middle zone. The products are not illegal to buy or own, but they are not approved for human use and so are not subject to the quality controls that govern pharmaceutical manufacturing."This might have happened in the US," Taylor says. "But consumers are at risk here in the UK, this is a global industry."He says a case like this demonstrates the magnitude of the risk, when "people think they are taking one product but it's actually something completely different"."So, they may also be getting additional side effects or different results that they can't explain."Murphy's wife Laura says her husband changed overnight. He had gone from a "loving partner" to a man who believed that she was "plotting" to take over his successful consulting business."One minute he would be crying and asking what was wrong with him, the next he would talk about wanting to take over Los Angeles," she says. "We had no history of mental illness in our family, Dan was so calm and stable before this happened."We did not know what to do."Life began to unravel. Murphy had an affair, was drinking copious amounts of alcohol, and felt his friends and family were out to get him - he even thought his mother-in-law wanted to murder him."I was in a full-blown psychosis - I believed that my loved ones were trying to hurt me and kill me," he recalls. "At this point, I've lost the plot. I'm not able to make any connection to the supplements, to anything that's happening."Then in December 2024, Murphy ran out of his supply of Paradigm Peptides supplements. It was then, he says, he felt his condition began to improve.Murphy and his family had no idea the FDA had been investigating the company, and it was not until February 2025 that he was told that the drugs he had been taking had been mixed with steroids."If only I had known, if the FDA had been more public, or even just put a notice on the Paradigm Peptides website. But instead, I'm taking this product and they know it's been cut with steroids," he says.So far, he says he seems to have made a full recovery. He is one of 167 of the victims who have come forward and sought a total of $78,317 (£58,169) compensation for the damage caused. Others had suffered blood clots, heart issues, anxiety and depression, the Department of Justice confirmed.Murphy says he realises now he was playing "Russian roulette" with his health and no longer takes supplements."Never again," he says, "and I'm speaking out now because I don't want people falling into the trap I fell into - that all supplements are safe. "I was gambling my health, my family and, in many respects, my life."

schema.headline: He bought a fitness supplement online to bulk up, but ended up losing his mind

title: Will Fifa president Gianni Infantino lose his job? If so, who comes in?
description: Infantino on the brink? Who might replace him if he goes?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Fifa president Gianni Infantino arrives for the Worl
body: Infantino on the brink? Who might replace him if he goes?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Fifa president Gianni Infantino arrives for the World Cup final on 19 JulyByChief football news reporterUpdated 6 hours agoLife moves fast for Fifa president Gianni Infantino.It was doing so last month as he was zig-zagging across the United States in a private jet to make him virtually omnipresent as the World Cup reached its crescendo.On 19 July he must have felt on top of the world as, together with US President Donald Trump, they handed the trophy over to Spain.Less than two weeks later, Infantino is in a lonely place after scrapping controversial plans to sell off stakes in Fifa competitions to private investment.Condemned by UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, castigated by fans of the game he professes to want to protect. These can easily be deflected as hazards of the job.Less so the threatened boycott of Fifa competitions by European governing body Uefa, and its subsequent stunning statement in which it declared it had lost confidence in Infantino's leadership.Concacaf (North and Central America and the Caribbean) and the AFC (Asia) also - in their own ways - have offered withering assessments of how Fifa is being run under Infantino."This issue extends far beyond a single proposal," said the AFC. "Rather, it has exposed fundamental weaknesses in Fifa's consultation and decision-making processes that must now be addressed."Sources say, in addition to rejecting Infantino's plan, the vast majority of the Concacaf members are either losing faith in the Fifa president's ability to govern the game, or have lost it altogether.On top of that, Carlos Cordeiro, special adviser to Infantino and appointed by Trump as senior adviser to the White House Task Force on the 2026 World Cup, has resigned.Fifa's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said in a statement to Associated Press that Fifa's own administration was "deceived" about the project.BBC Sport has approached Fifa for comment.It feels as though the walls are closing in on Infantino.But if this is the beginning of the end of his tenure, who takes over?Might Infantino really go?Firstly, it is wise to be realistic.Speaking to BBC Sport earlier this week, former Football Association chairman David Bernstein said of Infantino: "In a normal organisation, if he has to back down due to something of this magnitude he'd probably be shown the door."But Fifa is not a normal organisation. If he has the support of enough of the national associations, he will continue."Former Fifa vice-president Jim Boyce said he thought Infantino would "still have enough support" to be re-elected but "if things continue at the pace they are continuing, who knows?"He added: "If I was a betting man, which I'm not, I would still bet he will get his final four-year term."Infantino has been Fifa president since 2016. Before that he was secretary general of Uefa for seven years. Few know the map of football politics better than him.Now 56, Infantino became president by beating Asian Football Confederation president Sheikh Salman al-Khalifa by 115 votes to 88. His task was to clean up an organisation tainted by corruption allegations following the resignation of predecessor Sepp Blatter. Blatter was cleared of corruption charges last year."I will work tirelessly to bring football back to Fifa and Fifa back to football," said Infantino at the time.He has twice been re-elected unopposed, and it was expected the same thing would happen again next March. This is not unusual. Blatter was unopposed in 2007 and 2011.Brazilian Joao Havelange was the last person to unseat a Fifa president in an election, ousting Sir Stanley Rous in 1974. No-one opposed Havelange for five straight terms until he finally resigned in 1998, aged 82.Letters of support backing Infantino's re-election have been submitted. Will they be withdrawn?Who might replace him?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Concacaf president Victor Montagliani consoles Lionel Messi after Argentina's World Cup final defeat by SpainVictor Montagliani (Concacaf president)Like Infantino, he was elected in 2016 promising governance reform. A former president of Canada Soccer, Montagliani was heavily involved in the build up to, and delivery of the 2026 World Cup, the first to be hosted by three nations. He is fluent in French, Italian and Spanish, as well as English.Explaining his decision to run for the Concacaf presidency, Montagliani told the BC Business website: "Like anything, when I decide to go, I go. I campaigned on my own dime for three months, went to see all 41 countries, from the US to Bonaire, a little island off Venezuela."Montagliani took the lead when Concacaf hosted an expanded Copa America in 2024 - in an interview with BBC Sport he rejected the idea it could become a regular occurrence. Politically strong, he smoothed relations around Arsene Wenger's attempt to gain support for a World Cup every two years and has never truly bought into the idea of a 64-team World Cup.At the Leaders conference in 2025, he outlined why he felt football was strong enough to ride out any storm."The game is bigger than world current leaders," he said. "Football will survive regimes. Does it cause a headache? Of course. You have to be realistic about that. That is the beauty of our game, it is bigger than any individual and country."Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa (AFC president)Initially elected in 2013, he was elected unopposed for a fourth term to run to 2027.The Bahraini has presided over significant growth within the Asian confederation, through the Champions League Elite, Champions League Two, the Challenge League and the Women's Champions League, which was launched in 2024-25. The Asian Cup has been expanded to 24 teams.Sheikh Salman signed off the brutal takedown of how Fifa is being run by Infantino and has carried with him a 46-member confederation, many of whom are aware the figures being offered by Infantino's plan are huge in terms of their overall football expenditure.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, PSG president Nasser Al-Khelaifi (left) with manager Luis Enrique after the Champions League final victory over Arsenal in MayNasser Al-Khelaifi (PSG president and chair of European Football Clubs)Al-Khelaifi took over as chairman of the European Clubs' Association in the aftermath of the other seismic event that threatened to pull the game apart - the ill-fated European Super League, which collapsed within 48 hours in 2021.Al-Khelaifi presided over a name change - to European Football Clubs. More importantly, he expanded it to more than 800 members. Of the biggest clubs, only Real Madrid remain outside.In theory, the Qatari would be a serious challenger to Infantino. But it seems he doesn't want the role. "He genuinely, genuinely, genuinely doesn't want the job," was the response of a source close to the 52-year-old when asked about the possibility on Thursday.Mattias Grafstrom (Fifa secretary general)Appointed in May 2024 and an increasingly influential voice around the Fifa table.Multi-lingual Grafstrom become Infantino's chief of staff following his election as president in 2016.Another very visual presence at the World Cup, he could be seen as being too close to Infantino - and the general feeling Fifa's next president needs to be a non-European might also count against him.Fifa's next president will be confirmed at the organisation's 77th Congress in Morocco next March. Candidates have until 18 November to put their names forward.

schema.headline: Will Fifa president Gianni Infantino lose his job? If so, who comes in?

title: Ex-catering workers claim they are owed thousands in unpaid wages
description: Chrissy Bell is a senior advisor with Acas and spent 10 years working on its helpline. Acas provides free, impartial advice to employees and employers
body: Chrissy Bell is a senior advisor with Acas and spent 10 years working on its helpline. Acas provides free, impartial advice to employees and employers on workplace rights and disputes.  "If someone is expecting their wages on a certain date and it doesn't arrive or it doesn't arrive in full, then if people haven't got savings, even a small amount of difference can be the difference between them paying their bills and not being able to pay them," says Chrissy. She has this advice to anyone who believes they have not been paid the correct amount,"Firstly, work out the amount you should have been paid. So check payslips, timesheets, contracts and the first step is to speak to the employers, as there may have been a genuine mistake."If this does not work, she suggests putting a more formal grievance in writing, setting out any evidence, including timesheets, and then giving the employer a reasonable chance to respond.Finally, she says if it is not resolved internally after a reasonable amount of time then the person should consider making a claim to an employment tribunal if they are owed outstanding wages."If someone gets an award at an employment tribunal then there are systems in place to help them enforce it if necessary," she says. Martha Lindeque declined to provide a statement, but the BBC understands that her position is that she strongly denies the allegations made by her ex-staff.

schema.headline: Ex-catering workers claim they are owed thousands in unpaid wages

title: Fifa World Cup plans: Pressure builds on Gianni Infantino as Concacaf call for 'full review'
description: Gianni Infantino's leadership of Fifa has been publicly questioned by football's governing bodies in Europe, North and Central America and the Caribbe
body: Gianni Infantino's leadership of Fifa has been publicly questioned by football's governing bodies in Europe, North and Central America and the Caribbean.Uefa and Concacaf both released statements on Saturday criticising the leadership at the world governing body after Infantino said Fifa would no longer proceed with the proposal to sell stakes in their competitions to private investors.Uefa, which governs European football, welcomed the decision to withdraw the plan, describing it as a "victory for the whole game". The body accused of Infantino of failing to deliver on promises, quoting a speech he gave when campaigning to become Fifa president in 2016.Concacaf, which oversees football in North, Central America and the Caribbean, followed Uefa in criticising the plans, saying "unity had prevailed" and that the proposals were a "symptom of leadership that has stopped putting football first". "This recent unilateral and egregious act of poor governance and leadership follows a pattern of missteps and similar behaviour. A full review of this leadership must now take place," a Concacaf statement read. Unlike Uefa, Concacaf did not mention Infantino by name. The fallout from the plans means Infantino is now under immense pressure as he seeks re-election for a fourth term as president at the Fifa Congress in March.Uefa were the first major governing body to react to Infantino's decision to drop the investment plans, saying the Swiss had failed to deliver on his promises. "The current Fifa leadership has not only lost Uefa's confidence but also that of many other members of the football family," Uefa's statement read."When Gianni Infantino asked for the trust and the votes of Fifa's member associations to elect him as their president in 2016, he said, 'Of course we have to be transparent'."He told the assembled stakeholders, 'The money of Fifa is your money. It's not the money of the Fifa president. You are the national associations and the money of Fifa has to serve for the development of football and not for anything else'."On both these promises, he has failed to deliver. The shabby, back room, opaque deal he hatched and tried to force through was anything but transparent."Later on Saturday, Concacaf joined Uefa in criticising Fifa leadership and said "accountability cannot be optional". "When people entrusted with protecting the game conclude they can no longer do so from within, the football family is entitled to ask how such a proposal was allowed to proceed and who bears responsibility for it," a Concacaf statement read.UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham - the first leader of a major country to call on Infantino to resign - said Fifa made "the right decision" to back down.Uefa had been highly critical of the proposals since they were first reported in the media on Tuesday.In a powerful, lengthy statement released several hours after Fifa announced it had scrapped the plans, Uefa said:it "cannot keep going on" with "secret schemes of fast-track timescales cooked up by faceless individuals and of dubious benefit to the game".those responsible for the plan should be identified and held to account.it would devise a plan "with its associations and in close co-operation with other confederations" to make sure this "cannot occur again".it would work with partners to "propose a new way of distributing resources through the existing Fifa Forward programme".It also accused Infantino of "failing to use associations' money for the benefit of the game"."We must start to use some of that money that is sat idle in Fifa's bank account to deliver the kick-start that the grassroots and the wider game need," the statement added."But we don't need to sell off the family silver to pay for it."This is a victory for the whole game. But it must not be the end of the story. "The proposal has gone. The task of rebuilding trust in Fifa has only just begun."Fifa has yet to respond to Uefa's statement.Concacaf, which hosted this year's World Cup, was critical of the Fifa leadership without naming Infantino.The governing body expressed concern at Infantino's plans on Thursday, after Uefa had voted to boycott World Cups if the Fifa plan proceeded.While they stopped short of expressing no confidence in the Swiss, Concacaf said a "full review" of Fifa's leadership should be undertaken. Concacaf said: the "future of the FIFA World Cup, the greatest asset in world football, was advanced outside every established governance framework, without transparency, consultation or due process".the plans were a "symptom of leadership that has stopped putting football first".Fifa is "not a private enterprise. It is a body held in trust for the game and its members. Those appointed to serve it carry a fiduciary duty, a duty of service over power. Where that duty is not upheld, accountability cannot be optional".They added the unity demonstrated by its 41 member associations this week "reaffirmed that when guided by courage, integrity and sound governance, the game will remain where it belongs: in the hands of football - not a single individual". The Football Association said it supports Uefa's position, adding: "It is time for a full and robust review of Fifa's leadership and governance to ensure that the global game is run transparently."Lise Klaveness, president of the Norwegian Football Federation, said it was "reassuring to be part of a strong and united Uefa throughout this process"."We must acknowledge the entire framework of international football co-operation was unnecessarily put at risk in pursuit of individual interests rather than the best interests of the game," a statement read."Going forward, all our efforts must be directed towards improving governance."This cannot end as merely another power struggle conducted behind closed doors or through bilateral discussions."The proposal - first reported in the media on Tuesday - was met with widespread criticism, with Uefa voting on Thursday to boycott World Cups if the plans went ahead.European football's governing body said the World Cup "cannot be treated as an investment product".Two other major confederations then spoke out against the plans.Concacaf, which governs football in North and Central America and the Caribbean - and hosted this summer's World Cup - said its members "rejected" the proposal, with sources saying the vast majority of associations from the region are losing, or have lost, faith in Infantino.The AFC said it stood in "solidarity" with Uefa and Concacaf, while Burnham said Infantino was "the wrong man" to lead Fifa.On Friday, Fifa's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said the governing body's own administration had been "deceived" about the project.Carlos Cordeiro, Infantino's senior adviser on global strategy and governance, resigned over the matter, saying the proposal was "a bad deal for football" and would "mortgage football's future".Fifa and Infantino wanted to create a commercial subsidiary to run its main events, including its World Cups, and external investors would have been able to buy stakes in it.It said it would "invite third parties to make minority, non-controlling investments" in a new subsidiary called Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE).In a 25-page document created by investment bank JP Morgan, it was made clear Fifa's tournaments would expand to hit an estimated increased payout of 24m euros (£20.5m) per member association in the 2035-39 cycle.In the document, the World Cup was described as the "most widely viewed" sporting event but Fifa, by contrast, was said to be "under-monetised".There was no mention of the women's game.Fifa said Thrive Eternal was expected to lead the proposed investor group for FFE, had it been approved.Thrive is an American venture capital firm founded by Joshua Kushner, the brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared.A report in the New York Post, which broke the story of the Fifa plan withdrawal, quoted an unnamed source saying the situation had become a "brand nightmare" for Kushner.

schema.headline: Fifa World Cup plans: Pressure builds on Gianni Infantino as Concacaf call for 'full review'

title: Gianni Infantino and five days that shook football - and the echoes of European Super League
description: Any hope Gianni Infantino might have had of tiptoeing away from the scene of his World Cup private-investment wreckage having sustained only minor dam
body: Any hope Gianni Infantino might have had of tiptoeing away from the scene of his World Cup private-investment wreckage having sustained only minor damage to his reputation disappeared on Saturday.Uefa - the governing body of European football - went straight for the head of world game, saying it had "lost confidence" in his leadership.It was one of the most ferocious statements ever aimed at the holder of that position.Words such as "shabby" and "secret schemes" spoke for themselves.It came after a dramatic five days for football that sparked memories of the European Super League debacle of 2021.The ESL was a splinter league formed by 12 of Europe's biggest clubs, including six from the Premier League.Former England defender Gary Neville echoed the thoughts of many when he referred to it as "pure greed". It quickly unravelled.Infantino's private-investment plan did not have a catchy title, and lasted two days longer than the ESL.But despite football's world governing body confirming the proposal was being withdrawn on Saturday, the infamy will linger much longer.At the top level, football is a vast, money-making enterprise. The sums players and executives earn is beyond the scope of 'ordinary' fans.But have we discovered there is a line that cannot be crossed?The question many have asked around Infantino's plan is tied into a separate - but critical - aspect of the fundamental reasons behind this week unravelling. Fifa is a not-for-profit organisation. It has huge financial reserves - over $2bn (£1.48bn) - and is expected to announce record revenues of about $15bn (£11.13bn) in relation to this summer's World Cup.Given that backdrop - and the reality some countries simply did not need the extra $40m (£29.67m) being offered for football development initiatives if they signed up to Infantino's plan by 19 September - many wondered why private investment was needed in the first place.It was a question that needed to be asked. But that did not happen in public  - or, it has become apparent, privately in Fifa's corridors of power.Many of Fifa's most senior people - from vice-presidents to special advisers and executives - did not have a chance to ask any questions, simply because they had no clue the plans were being drawn up.Uefa had strongly opposed the plans from the moment they became public. When they were dropped, its response was damning."The current Fifa leadership has not only lost Uefa's confidence but also that of many other members of the football family," it said in a statement."When Gianni Infantino asked for the trust and the votes of Fifa's member associations to elect him as their president in 2016, he said: 'Of course we have to be transparent.'"He told the assembled stakeholders: 'The money of Fifa is your money. It's not the money of the Fifa president. You are the national associations and the money of Fifa has to serve for the development of football and not for anything else.'"On both these promises, he has failed to deliver."It was not the first time a lack of transparency had been highlighted.Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa - president of the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), and one of eight Fifa vice-presidents - referred to it too.He said any future plans that may impact global football should be presented to members "in a timely, transparent and meaningful manner"."The future of global football must always be shaped through proper consultation, collective dialogue and respect for the established governance structures of our game," he added.Football Australia chair Anter Isaac said trust was earned "not simply through good decisions, but through the integrity of the processes that lead to them"."Football has never stood still, nor should it," he said. "Some principles, however, should never change. Integrity. Independence. Good governance. Transparency. Meaningful consultation. Due process. These are not constraints on progress."With the ESL, it was the fans that drew the line - backed by the Premier League, the Football Association and even Prince William.The plan in 2021 was for the clubs who took part to remain in their national leagues, but also to play each other in a new midweek European competition, which would have rivalled the Champions League.Critics argued it was a way for the clubs to enrich themselves in a closed league that would have increased  commercial and broadcasting income, and the principle of a domestic football pyramid should be protected.After 72 hours of criticism, the plans all but fell apart. In the aftermath, it was claimed clubs did not get the opportunity to present a rounded case because the outline plan was leaked to the media. That meant the reaction was so fierce any counter-argument would have been lost.This week has been remarkably similar - except this time, it was people in football who drew the line in the sand.The only real difference is Fifa did put its counterargument forward in the early hours of Friday - along with an assertion its "planned consultation process was disrupted by incorrect media reports".As with the ESL, by that point the direction of travel was already established and could not be changed.With sentiment so strongly against the plans, a damning statement from Fifa's respected chief operating officer Kevin Lamour would have been a crushing blow. He described the controversial plans as "the project of one person" and claimed Fifa's administration had been "deceived". BBC Sport has approached Fifa for comment.Lamour acknowledged he had a duty of loyalty to his employer but also to "certain values" and supporting his colleagues."Our mission - the mission of the hundreds of passionate, dedicated, and exemplary Fifa employees - is to serve football," he wrote."If that means I lose my job, then so be it. I will understand and respect that decision. "At least I'll sleep well tonight."Infantino has developed a close relationship with US President Donald Trump, and the pair helped present the World Cup to Spain less than a fortnight ago.If Infantino was looking for assistance from Trump when he was asked about the proposals for the first time on Friday, he did not get it. Trump said he had not spoken to the 56-year-old about the plans.A report in the New York Post, which broke the story of the plans being withdrawn, quoted an unnamed source saying the situation had become a "brand nightmare" for Joshua Kushner - brother of Trump's son-in-law Jared.Kusher founded Thrive Eternal - the American venture capital firm that would have led the proposed investor group had Fifa's plans gone ahead.As with the ESL, in the end, Infantino was left with no choice but to withdraw the idea.Now he is left to clear up the mess and build bridges, amid claims support for his re-election as Fifa president in March is receding.Speaking before Uefa's statement on Saturday, its vice-president Laura McAllister spoke to BBC Radio Four's Today programme."All of the confederations will be considering options now," she said."There will be moves, I'm sure, to encourage people to stand, but it's early days yet."The key thing this week has been to defeat this proposal with unity and consensus and that's what we've been able to do."Once again, football has shown that while it is prepared to accept many things - and not all of them will be popular - there are some lines that cannot be crossed.

schema.headline: Gianni Infantino and five days that shook football - and the echoes of European Super League

title: Remains of Roman port found behind woman's home in East Yorkshire
description: Figure caption, Twelve Roman buildings discovered beneath woman's paddockByJosh Gorroño Chapmanin BroughThe remains of what is believed to be a Roman
body: Figure caption, Twelve Roman buildings discovered beneath woman's paddockByJosh Gorroño Chapmanin BroughThe remains of what is believed to be a Roman port have been dug up on land behind a woman's home.Archaeologists said they had found evidence of 12 buildings beneath a paddock close to the Humber estuary, in Brough, East Yorkshire.Melanie Stanford, who owns the land, said it had come as a complete surprise to learn of the scale of the Roman settlement.Dr Peter Halkon, site director, said the town was ideally located as a trading point, with access to York and the European continent.Image source, Josh Gorroño Chapman/BBCImage caption, Dr Peter Halkon says Brough was ideally located as a trading pointBrough is thought to be on the site of Petuaria, the tribal capital of the Parisi, who lived in eastern Yorkshire during the Roman period.Halkon, 70, is leading the community dig for the Petuaria ReVisited Project, external, which was set up in 2018 to shed more light on the town's Roman past.He said the buildings would likely have been used to store goods taken off ships.Other artefacts found there included pottery, animal bones and oyster shells."The Romans were incredibly fond of oysters," he said.Roman walls in the area have been known about since the 1930s, but digs in recent years have led to new discoveries, including a Roman forum and a theatre.Image source, Josh Gorroño Chapman/BBCImage caption, Archaeologists made the discovery close to the Humber estuaryStanford said she was approached for permission to carry out a dig after ground-penetrating radar revealed the buildings."I said yes, let's see what's there."It's fascinating – I'm loving coming down here. I'm not doing the digging, I just enjoy watching."I'm learning more now and it's really exciting," she added. "With 12 buildings they might be coming back next year to do some more."Volunteer James Newbound, who is studying archaeology at university, said the experience had been really enjoyable."Once you get the bug, you just have to keep going, because it's stuff that's never been seen since it was buried."Listen to highlights from Hull and East Yorkshire on BBC Sounds, watch the latest episode of Look North.Get in touchYour Voice

title: Bev Craig: Who is the new Mayor of Greater Manchester?
description: Image source, Labour PartyImage caption, Bev Craig has been elected as the new mayor of Greater ManchesterByLauren HirstNorth West and Kevin Fitzpatri
body: Image source, Labour PartyImage caption, Bev Craig has been elected as the new mayor of Greater ManchesterByLauren HirstNorth West and Kevin FitzpatrickBBC Manchester political reporterBev Craig will succeed UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham as Greater Manchester's mayor after winning Thursday's by-election.The Labour candidate claimed victory after securing 309,525 votes over Reform's Sian Astley who won 157,178.Burnham stood down after winning the Makerfield by-election in June to return to the House of Commons. He subsequently became prime minister on 20 July.But who is Bev Craig, what has she done, and what does she stand for? Will she closely follow her predecessor's agenda or does she have different priorities for a city region which consists of 10 boroughs and is home to more than two million people?Having grown up on a council estate in Belfast, Craig moved to Manchester in 2003 at the age of 18 to study politics and modern history at the University of Manchester.After graduating, she began her career in local government. She went on to work in higher education and then at a national trade union, leading on social care.Craig was first elected as a councillor for the Burnage ward on Manchester City Council in 2011.She was executive member for adult social care and health throughout the Covid-19 global pandemic, before becoming deputy council leader in 2021.Craig soon took over as leader when Sir Richard Leese stood down after 25 years in the role.Her promotion made her the local authority's first female boss and the council's first openly gay leader.The 41-year-old has also held the role of deputy mayor for economy, business and inclusive growth on the Greater Manchester Combined Authority.She was made an Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in the New Year Honours List in 2025 for services to local government.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Craig, pictured with her partner Tracy, on polling day on Thursday Key achievements and challengesAs council leader, Craig has overseen sustained annual economic growth in Manchester of more than 3% during the last decade, making it one of the fastest growing city economies in Europe.The main criticism since Craig became council leader has been around the lack of affordable housing at a time when skyscrapers have been built in the city centre. Although, in her tenure the local authority has built social housing for the first time in 40 years.In November 2025, children's services in Manchester were rated as "outstanding" by inspectors after a decade-long process of improvement. The service had been rated "inadequate" by Ofsted in 2014 and it was not until 2022 that it was deemed to be "good".However, an issue that has brought negative headlines during Craig's career has been crime and anti-social behaviour, notably in the city centre's flagship communal area of Piccadilly Gardens. The latest in a long line of multi-million pound plans to revamp it was launched in February 2026 and work is under way to make it "an attractive world-class space". Despite a high-profile policing operation, regular incidents of violence still occur there.Image caption, Bev Craig became leader of Manchester City Council five years agoWhat has she promised?After she was announced as Labour's candidate to succeed Westminster-bound Burnham, Craig said she was ready to "deliver the next chapter for the region".Her headline campaign pledges have been to freeze Metrolink and bus fares on the Bee Network and extend free bus travel to 11 to 18-year-olds. Currently, only 16 to 18-year-olds benefit from the scheme.She said: "I will work every day for us to make sure everyone shares in the success Greater Manchester is building - making sure there's more money in people's pockets, pride in every town centre with a New High Streets Fund, a new generation of council and affordable homes, and an expanded Bee Network that freezes fares and that works for all of us."She said she was committed to delivering 50,000 new homes in a mix of council properties and genuinely affordable housing over the next 15 years. Craig said she would also launch a new £20m high street scheme, promising it would support small businesses, revitalise empty units and invest in town-centre regeneration.Labour Party's Bev Craig's mayoral candidate interviewBBC Radio Manchester interviewed each candidate in the mayoral by-election.

schema.headline: Bev Craig: Who is the new Mayor of Greater Manchester?

title: Greater Manchester's mayor Bev Craig says PM's new powers will change lives
description: Figure caption, The by-election was called after Andy Burnham was elected as MP for Makerfield in Greater Manchester in JuneByJuliet Sarah Phillips an
body: Figure caption, The by-election was called after Andy Burnham was elected as MP for Makerfield in Greater Manchester in JuneByJuliet Sarah Phillips and Stewart WhittinghamNorth WestUpdated 3 hours agoGreater Manchester's new Mayor Bev Craig has said Prime Minister Andy Burnham's move to give the regions more power could "change our lives".The Labour candidate claimed victory in Thursday's by-election after securing 309,525 votes over Reform's Sian Astley, who won 157,178.The 41-year-old will succeed Burnham as mayor, after he stood down to run in the Makerfield by-election in June. The pair appeared together at a Labour rally in Manchester after Craig's election win.Craig said: "For a prime minister two weeks in, to start giving powers out of Whitehall and putting it in the places that can make a difference - that can change our lives."She added: "I will rise to his challenge about taking the power and control that he is offering mayors like me to make our regions better."Because that is what it is all about."Burnham has said he would give all mayors of city regions in England a share of income tax revenue for the first time, as part of his drive to transfer power from Westminster to local leaders.Opposition parties said the plans lacked detail and could lead to areas with weaker economies losing out on funding.Bur Craig said she was "excited" about the challenge and would not "stop at the levels of growth that we have achieved".She said she wanted to make "every kid" in Greater Manchester "feel they can succeed".Image caption, Bev Craig spoke in front of a Labour audience after she was elected as mayorThe prime minister said Manchesterism was about "devolution" and "taking control of things that affect people's daily lives, such as housing, building more homes that people can truly afford and the buses"."We want everyone in Greater Manchester facing the same way, pulling in the same way," he said."It is a different way of doing things."Burnham told Craig "go further and do more" as he dubbed her the "queen of the north".He added: "You are the right person to lead this great city region forward into its best decade ever, because that is what the next decade is going to be."Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Craig, pictured with her partner Tracy, on polling day on Thursday More than two million people across Greater Manchester's 10 boroughs were eligible to vote in the mayoral contest but turnout was just under 25%.Reform's Astley said after her defeat: "I'm really proud of our campaign, of getting out there, working with all the branches and councillors to try and get people motivated to get out and vote."She added "we'll be watching to see if all those pledges made during the campaign are delivered".Craig grew up on a council estate in Belfast, but moved to Manchester in 2003 at the age of 18 to study politics and modern history at the University of Manchester.What has she promised?After she was announced as Labour's candidate to succeed Westminster-bound Burnham, Craig said she was ready to "deliver the next chapter for the region".Her headline campaign pledges have been to freeze Metrolink and bus fares on the Bee Network and extend free bus travel to 11 to 18-year-olds. Currently, only 16 to 18-year-olds benefit from the scheme.She said she was committed to delivering 50,000 new homes in a mix of council properties and genuinely affordable housing over the next 15 years. Craig said she would also launch a new £20m high street scheme, promising it would support small businesses, revitalise empty units and invest in town-centre regeneration.Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Greater Manchester

title: William and Kate bring children to Commonwealth Games netball and cycling events
description: Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The Prince and Princess of Wales laugh with British cyclist Laura Kenny while sitting behind Olympic champion Sir
body: Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The Prince and Princess of Wales laugh with British cyclist Laura Kenny while sitting behind Olympic champion Sir Chris HoyByMary McCoolBBC ScotlandReporting fromGlasgowUpdated 31 minutes agoThe Prince and Princess of Wales have brought their three children to watch some of the final sporting events at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.Cheering crowds at the city's OVO Hydro were treated to exhilarating performances in the netball semi-finals where the family watched New Zealand's 61-54 win over England.They then made their way to the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome - where they chatted to British cyclist Laura Kenny and sat one row behind Olympic cycling champion, Sir Chris.Known as the Duke and Duchess of Rothesay while in Scotland, the couple also spent time meeting athletes, staff and volunteers during a slightly blustery visit to the venue on the River Clyde.They met gold medal-winning para powerlifter Mark Swan and gymnast Reuben Ward on the concourse.Princess Catherine and Charlotte also took the time to take photos with the Team Scotland netball players - who lost to Uganda on Thursday, missing their chance to finish third.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The family left the Hydro to meet Games volunteers and athletesImage source, PA MediaImage caption, Games mascot Finnie gives George and Charlotte a chuckle as the family meet hard-working Games volunteersImage source, PA MediaImage caption, Charlotte and Finnie exchange a high fiveImage source, PA MediaImage caption, Princess Catherine and Charlotte watch the action on the court at Glasgow's OVO HydroImage source, PA MediaImage caption, Team Scotland's netball team sat behind the Royal familyImage source, PA MediaImage caption, Prince William chatted animatedly to athletes during the gameImage source, PA MediaImage caption, Shock, applause and a great deal of excitement in the stands during Saturday's netball semi-final between England and New ZealandImage source, PA MediaImage caption, Louis listens intently to his father William, while George's attention remains on the matchSaturday's netball results mean Jamaica and New Zealand will battle it out for the gold on Sunday during some of the final medal awards of the tournament.England will also try to deny Australia a consolation bronze, before teams transform the Hydro from a netball court back to a gig venue for the closing ceremony on Sunday night.The venue will be turned around in just six hours.It has been a scaled-down version of the Games, with 215 medals awarded across 10 sports, however it has hosted a record 47 para-sports events.Glasgow stepped in to host the tournament - for the second time in eight years - when Australian state Victoria pulled out due to soaring costs.King Charles and Queen Camilla emerged from a Tardis during the spectacular opening ceremony last Thursday.Flags from 74 nations and territories were carried into the arena during the event, which also featured the Loch Ness monster and performances from Nathan Evans, Tom Walker and KT Tunstall.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The Duchess and Charlotte post for a photo with the Team Scotland women's netball teamImage source, PA MediaImage source, PA MediaImage caption, The youngest of the children Louis enjoys himself at the Sir Chris Hoy VelodromeSimple Minds are due to perform at the closing ceremony alongside Scottish performers Cammy Barnes, BEMZ and Sandi Thom.Organisers say it will "highlight the people who made the Games possible, the pride of the host city and the iconic sporting triumphs".The curtain call will also be played out by Highland folk and electronic band Elephant Sessions, while Scottish singer Shereen Cutkelvin will mark the ceremonial flag handover.Ahmedabad in the west of India is set to host the centenary Commonwealth Games in 2030.Shankar Mahadevan, one of Bollywood's greatest vocalists, and actress Rashmika Mandanna are set to take to the stage as the baton is passed over.Australian artist Delta Goodrem will perform a homage to Scotland at the closing ceremony 20 years after she sang in Melbourne 2006.Community groups and cultural organisations will also be involved.

schema.headline: William and Kate bring children to Commonwealth Games netball and cycling events

title: EastEnders star Shane Richie facing drink-drive charge
description: EastEnders actor Shane Richie is to appear in court charged with drink-driving, police have said.Essex Police confirmed it was called to reports of a
body: EastEnders actor Shane Richie is to appear in court charged with drink-driving, police have said.Essex Police confirmed it was called to reports of a suspected drink-driver in the Church Langley Way area of Harlow, shortly before 23:20 BST on Wednesday.A force spokesman confirmed the 62-year-old, of Tadworth, Surrey, was arrested and a charge of drink-driving had been authorised against him.It added Richie, real name Shane Roche, was due to appear at Colchester Magistrates' Court on 9 September. Richie plays Alfie Moon in EastEnders, making his first appearance in the BBC soap in 2002.The Sun reported he was arrested, external at a Tesco petrol station forecourt.Essex Police said: "Officers were called to reports of a suspected drink-driver in the area of Church Langley Way, Harlow, shortly before 23:20 on Wednesday, 29 July."On arrival, officers arrested a man."A charge of drink-driving has subsequently been authorised against Shane Roche, 62, of Tadworth, Surrey."Richie's representative has been contacted for comment.Do you have a story suggestion for Essex? Contact us below.
